newsitem.title: UK: Stg strength sapped amid more sober rate view.
newsitem.headline: Stg strength sapped amid more sober rate view.

text.p: The pound extended Monday's sharp slide in European trading, losing up to one percent against a trade-weighted basket of currencies as market players began to adopt a more sober outlook for UK interest rates.
Analysts said a wave of uncertainty has entered the currency market as extreme forecasts of up to 8.0 percent UK base lending rates by year-end are being toned down.

Domestic press commentary has begun hand-wringing about the potential for recession early next year if interest rates and sterling are rammed even higher and exporter calls for a cap on the currency's recent surge have sharpened.

"What we're seeing is a reassessment of some of the more exaggerated interest rate forecasts and sterling is no longer the one-way bet it once seemed," said Neil Parker, treasury economist at Royal Bank of Scotland.

Parker said the short-sterling interest rate futures contract is now showing rates peaking about 7.25 percent compared with 6.75 percent at present. "This is much more reasonable than some of the talk we've seen recently," he said.

Sterling fell to as low as 2.9745 marks in late trade on Tuesday, down almost four pfennigs from 3.0130/40 late Monday and down 3.7 percent from near eight-year highs set last week. It settled slightly off its lows about 1500 GMT.
Against the dollar, the pound was trading at $1.6306/16 compared with $1.6321/26 late Monday. Its trade-weighted index fell to as low as 103.6 from 104.6 at yesterday's close.

The sharp sterling retreat this week is expected to herald a long-awaited stabilisation of the currency after months of remorseless gains. But support is expected on dips under 2.95 marks for now until the outcome of the Bank of England's next monetary policy council meeting on August 6 and 7 is seen.
"Sterling had a fantastic rally, and if you put that into context, yesterday's fall was not quite as dramatic as it looked at first sight," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.
The sell-off Monday was partly prompted by talk the Bank of England might hold off another rate rise at next week's meeting.

Traders also pointed to thin market conditions, which tend to exaggerate market movements. The extension of the slide today was exacerbated by rumbling talk of higher German and Dutch interest rates and a modest recovery of the mark.
Paul Meggyesi, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said sterling may dip a little more in the short term, especially if the mark benefits further from short-covering.
"But the time may not yet be ripe for a full-blown trend reversal," he said.
Predictions of a recession in UK manufacturing due to the strength of the pound were a bit alarmist and ignored the effect of rising domestic demand on growth, he said.
Consumer credit data for July released on Tuesday showed another sharp rise. Consumer credit rose 1.275 billion sterling, against a one billion increase expected by economists.

Yet analysts said much of the consumer boom currently being cited is related to the windfall cash gains from savers who received free shares following a rash of stock market flotations of former UK building societies.
"The long-term effect of this largely once-off injection of cash is still very unclear," said Parker at RBS.
Parker said monetary policy is already extremely tight and the Bank of England's remit from the Treasury means its inflation target must be balanced against government growth objectives.
Real, or inflation-adjusted, UK interest rates are already between 4.5 and 5.0 percent, the pound is at multi-year highs and public spending limits remain very tight.
Further sharp tightening of policy may risk monetary overkill, he said.
-- Mike Dolan, London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
